title: Is the Culture in Your School Killing You?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles argues that culture is the central problem for school leaders precisely because it is invisible to those immersed in it. Shared assumptions become so innate that people stop recognising them, so solutions obvious to an outsider cannot be seen from inside. He makes the case through two stories: David Foster Wallace's fish who do not know what water is, and the French defeat at Crecy in 1346, where a chivalric culture of bravery drove fifteen futile charges against English longbowmen. The French king could have regrouped but his culture would not let him see that option, while Edward III had spent years changing English culture to fit a changing world. The move is to use narrative rather than data to make the point that culture must adapt and that changing it can change outcomes. It is a short, rhetorical piece with a clear call to step out of the water and get a new perspective.
points: The most obvious and important realities of a school culture are the hardest to see and talk about, a phenomenon the author links to habituation.
Leaders and professionals inside a school often cannot see solutions that would be obvious to an outsider, which is true of all organisations.
The Crecy story shows a once-successful culture becoming lethal when it prevents leaders from changing course despite clear evidence.
Edward III's eight years of mandatory longbow practice stands as the counter-example of deliberately shaping culture ahead of a changing world.
The practical invitation is to get out of the water by gaining an outside perspective before the culture makes decisions for you.
quotes: Culture itself is the problem: we are immersed in it, and our shared assumptions in a school are so innate that we stop recognising them. (Cognitive scientists call this process habituation). Solutions which are obvious to an outsider are invisible to the leaders and professionals in a school.
The point of the fish story is merely that the most obvious, important realities are often the ones that are hardest to see and talk about.
Philip ordered his army to halt on a hill facing the English. But the culture of chivalry valued bravery. No group would risk losing face by not reaching the enemy first.
Philip could have regrouped. But chivalric culture demanded bravery, so he ordered his cavalry to charge, hacking down their own crossbowmen blocking their path.

But a culture which had succeeded for hundreds of years didn’t let him see this. He and his princes and knights couldn’t see the obvious and they charged, and charged, and charged again, well into the night.
Edward realised culture has to adapt because the world is constantly changing. Even more importantly, he realised changing the culture has the power to change the world.
